query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The corrosion resistance of steels in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily due to the rapid formation and self-healing of a chromium‐rich passive oxide layer. This film is maintained and repaired by accelerated Cr diffusion along grain boundaries, which is enhanced in a refined (ultrafine-grained) microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional stainless steel (e.g., Fe–Cr alloy) with a coarse-grained microstructure and standard Cr content that forms a passive oxide film under service conditions.
generation.intervention: Apply a grain refinement treatment (such as severe plastic deformation) to produce an ultrafine-grained (UFG) version of the steel, thus increasing the density of grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Expose both coarse-grained (baseline) and UFG-treated steel samples to a controlled simulated environment representative of chemical processing and nuclear power conditions – for example, aqueous chloride or acidified solutions at elevated temperature (around 300°C) under static/dynamic flow conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: An enhanced network of grain boundaries acting as fast diffusion pathways for Cr atoms, leading to a thicker and more uniform Cr2O3 passive film on the steel surface.
generation.mechanism: The ultrafine-grained structure accelerates Cr transport from the bulk to the surface. When the passive film is locally damaged by corrosive agents, the high density of grain boundaries facilitates prompt Cr segregation and continuous reformation of the protective oxide film, thereby suppressing further corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline coarse-grained steel, the UFG-treated steel should show (1) a faster and more complete formation of a Cr-enriched passive film, (2) lower corrosion current densities measured by electrochemical techniques, and (3) reduced pit initiation/growth in localized corrosion tests.
generation.baseline: Coarse-grained stainless steel with conventional passive film formation leading to moderate corrosion rates under identical test conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be valid for steels with sufficient Cr content (typically >10 wt%) operating in moderately aggressive environments (e.g., aqueous media typical of chemical processing or nuclear plant water chemistry) at temperatures up to about 300°C, where grain-boundary diffusion remains effective. In extremes outside these conditions (e.g., very high temperature or atypical chemical exposures), other factors may dominate the corrosion behavior.
generation.uncertainty: While enhanced grain-boundary diffusion is expected to improve passive film repair, the exact quantitative improvement in corrosion resistance and the impact of potential interactions with other alloying elements or impurities remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical stainless steel samples – one set maintaining the as-cast/coarse-grained microstructure (baseline) and another processed via severe plastic deformation to achieve an ultrafine-grained structure. Subject both sets to cyclic corrosion testing in a simulated chemical-processing/nuclear-power environment (e.g., an aqueous chloride solution maintained at ~300°C under controlled flow conditions) for a defined duration.
measurements: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to quantify corrosion current densities and assess passive film stability
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to measure passive film thickness and Cr enrichment
Microscopic imaging (e.g., SEM) to evaluate pit density and morphology on the surface
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the UFG-treated samples do not display significantly enhanced Cr enrichment in the passive film, thicker/more uniform oxide layers, and lower corrosion rates (as measured by EIS and pit analysis) compared to the coarse-grained baseline, the hypothesis that grain-boundary–accelerated Cr diffusion is the primary mechanism for corrosion resistance would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Early research reported that stainless steel, Fe-Cr alloy, and CrFe15Ni15 alloy have excellent corrosion resistance due to the dense Cr2O3 passivation film formed on the surface [,,]. Similarly, it was speculated that the Cr2O3 passivation film has the same effect in the corrosion resistance of HEAs. AlCoCrFeNi [], AlxCrFe1.5MnNi0.5 [], and Al0.5CoCrCuFeNiBx [] verified the foregoing speculation. Therefore, for the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating passivation film of this study, it can be obtained from the results of XPS that the Cr2O3 in the passivation film provides good corrosion resistance for the coating, and the addition of trace amount of Nb results in forming a stable metal oxide of Nb2O5 in the passivation film of the coating, which also plays a positive role in the corrosion resistance [,].

Corrosion in molten salts is affected by several factors such as thermodynamics of corrosion reactions, elemental activities in the salt and the alloy, impurities, and temperature gradients. For instance, moisture in the salt can lead to the formation of hydrofluoric acid which can interact with metallic structural alloys and cause elemental dissolution into the salt. Also, metallic impurities incorporated in the salt may undergo exchange reactions to leach the least noble element out of the alloy. Most engineering alloys used in nuclear applications contain reasonable amounts of Cr to provide protection against air oxidation, and typically, chromium is the most vulnerable alloying element to fluoride salt corrosion.
